documents.description: The Mekong giant catfish (Pangasianodon gigas) is one of the world's largest freshwater fish and a Critically Endangered species of the Mekong basin.

documents.name: Midwife Toad
documents.description: Explore midwife toads (genus Alytes): small European toads in which the male wraps strings of eggs around his hind legs and carries them until they are ready to hatch.

documents.name: Millipede
documents.description: Explore millipedes (class Diplopoda): slow, many-legged arthropods with two leg pairs per segment that recycle leaf litter and curl up or release chemicals to defend themselves.

documents.name: Mite
documents.description: Mites are tiny arachnids in the subclass Acari. Meet the harmless red velvet mite (Trombidium) and learn how diverse and varied this ancient group really is.

documents.name: Ocean Sunfish (Mola)
documents.description: Explore the ocean sunfish (Mola mola): the heaviest bony fish in the world — a huge, disc-shaped, almost tailless fish that basks at the surface and feeds largely on jellyfish.

documents.name: Mole
documents.description: Explore moles (family Talpidae): small, powerful burrowing mammals with spade-like front paws and velvety fur that spend almost their whole lives digging through soil.

documents.name: Naked Mole-Rat
documents.description: Explore the naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber): a near-hairless burrowing rodent of East Africa that lives in insect-like colonies with a queen — and is famous for extreme longevity.

documents.name: Monarch Butterfly
documents.description: Learn about the monarch butterfly, its multi-generational migration, milkweed-feeding caterpillars, and why this iconic insect is of conservation concern.

documents.name: Mongoose
documents.description: Explore mongooses (family Herpestidae): small, agile carnivores of Africa and Asia, from solitary species to highly social groups like the banded mongoose and meerkat.

documents.name: Monitor Lizard
documents.description: Monitor lizards (genus Varanus) are large, active reptiles. A group-level overview using the Nile monitor as a reference — habitat, diet, behaviour, and the Komodo dragon link.

documents.name: Moose
documents.description: Moose (Alces alces): the largest living deer. An educational overview of its northern forest habitat, browsing diet, antlers, and solitary behaviour.

documents.name: Moray Eel
documents.description: Explore moray eels (family Muraenidae): reef-dwelling predatory fish with a second set of hidden jaws, often seen peering from crevices with their mouths open to breathe.

documents.name: Moth
documents.description: Explore moths (order Lepidoptera): a vast, mostly night-flying group of insects — far more numerous than butterflies — that pollinate plants and feed much of the food web.

documents.name: Motmot
documents.description: Explore motmots (family Momotidae): colourful Neotropical birds with distinctive racket-tipped tails they swing like pendulums — using the turquoise-browed motmot as a reference.

documents.name: Mountain Goat
documents.description: Learn about the mountain goat, a white, shaggy-coated alpine mammal of steep cliffs in parts of northwestern North America, and why it is not a true goat.

documents.name: Mouse
documents.description: Group-level profile of the small rodents called mice: the house mouse Mus musculus, the wild European wood mouse, how mice differ from rats and voles, and why wild, commensal and laboratory mice are not the same thing.

documents.name: Mousebird
documents.description: Explore mousebirds (order Coliiformes): crested, long-tailed African birds that scramble mouse-like through bushes, hang and sunbathe in clusters, and are the only bird order unique to Africa.

documents.name: Mudpuppy
documents.description: Explore the mudpuppy (Necturus maculosus): a fully aquatic North American salamander that keeps bushy external gills for life — harmless, despite myths, and an indicator of clean water.

documents.name: Mudskipper
documents.description: Explore mudskippers (e.g. Periophthalmus): amphibious gobies that breathe through the skin, walk on their fins, and spend much of their lives out of water on tropical mudflats.

documents.name: Mule
documents.description: A mule is not a species but a first-generation hybrid: a donkey sire crossed with a horse dam. With 63 chromosomes it is effectively always sterile, combining donkey sure-footedness with horse size.

documents.name: Muriqui
documents.description: Explore muriquis (genus Brachyteles): the largest monkeys in the Americas — gentle, egalitarian 'woolly spider monkeys' of Brazil's Atlantic Forest. Critically Endangered.

documents.name: Mushroom Coral
documents.description: Explore mushroom corals (Fungia and relatives): unusual stony corals that live as a single large, free-living polyp, often able to right themselves and even move a little.

documents.name: Musk Deer
documents.description: Musk deer (genus Moschus) are small, antlerless hoofed mammals of forested and alpine parts of Asia. Learn their biology, ecology, and conservation concerns.

documents.name: Mussel
documents.description: Learn about mussels, bivalve molluscs like the blue mussel (Mytilus edulis). Explore their shells, byssal threads, filter feeding, habitat, and ecological role.

documents.name: Nautilus
documents.description: Explore the chambered nautilus (Nautilus pompilius): a shelled cephalopod and living fossil with dozens of tentacles, jet propulsion, and a gas-filled spiral shell.

documents.name: Nectar Bat
documents.description: Nectar bats (e.g. Glossophaginae) feed on nectar with long tongues and can pollinate night-blooming plants like agave and some cacti in specific regions.

documents.name: Newt
documents.description: Newts are small semi-aquatic salamanders. A group-level overview using the smooth newt as a reference — life cycle, habitat, and why wild amphibians should not be handled.

documents.name: Nightjar
documents.description: Explore nightjars (family Caprimulgidae): superbly camouflaged nocturnal birds that catch insects on the wing and churr through the night — using the European nightjar as a reference.

documents.name: Nile Crocodile
documents.description: The Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) is a large crocodilian of African rivers and wetlands. Learn about its biology, behaviour, ecology and role.

documents.name: Nile Perch
documents.description: Learn about the Nile perch (Lates niloticus), a large African freshwater predator native to the Nile and other systems, and a notorious invader in Lake Victoria.

documents.name: Nudibranch
documents.description: Explore nudibranchs (order Nudibranchia): dazzling shell-less sea slugs whose bright colours warn of borrowed stings and toxins, beloved by divers and photographers.

documents.name: Numbat
documents.description: Explore the numbat (Myrmecobius fasciatus): a small, striped, termite-eating marsupial of Western Australia — uniquely day-active among marsupials, and Endangered in the wild.

documents.name: Oarfish
documents.description: Explore the oarfish (Regalecus glesne): the longest bony fish in the world, a ribbon-like deep-sea giant rarely seen alive — and the likely source of many 'sea serpent' legends.

documents.name: Ocelot
documents.description: Explore the ocelot (Leopardus pardalis): a sleek, chain-rosetted wild cat of the American tropics — a nocturnal hunter once devastated by the fur trade, now recovering in many areas.

documents.name: Octopus
documents.description: Octopuses (order Octopoda): cephalopod molluscs with eight arms, complex behaviour and camouflage. Common octopus as a reference species and a cautious behavioural summary.

documents.name: Okapi
documents.description: Explore the okapi (Okapia johnstoni): the giraffe's only living relative, a secretive striped forest mammal of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and a conservation priority.

documents.name: Olingo
documents.description: Explore olingos (genus Bassaricyon): slender, nocturnal, tree-living members of the raccoon family from the American tropics — often confused with the kinkajou but without a grasping tail.

documents.name: Olm
documents.description: Explore the olm (Proteus anguinus): a pale, blind, fully aquatic cave salamander of European karst caves that keeps its larval gills for life and can live for decades — even a century.

documents.name: Oncilla
documents.description: Explore the oncilla (Leopardus tigrinus): one of the smallest wild cats in the Americas — a delicate, spotted, little-known forest hunter facing growing conservation concern.

documents.name: Orangutan
documents.description: Explore the orangutans (genus Pongo): great apes of Borneo and Sumatra, their arboreal life, fruit-based diet, remarkable intelligence, and why all species are conservation priorities.

documents.name: Orca (Killer Whale)
documents.description: Explore the orca (Orcinus orca): the ocean's top predator and the largest member of the dolphin family — a highly intelligent, deeply social animal with distinct cultures and dialects.

documents.name: Orchid Bee
documents.description: Orchid bees (tribe Euglossini) are brilliant metallic bees of the Neotropics. Males collect floral scents; some are pollinators of certain orchids and plants.

documents.name: Osprey
documents.description: The osprey (Pandion haliaetus) is the only living member of the family Pandionidae, a near-cosmopolitan raptor built almost entirely around catching live fish.

documents.name: Ostrich
documents.description: Explore the ostrich (Struthio camelus): the world's largest and heaviest living bird, a fast-running flightless ratite of African grasslands and semi-deserts.

documents.name: Otter
documents.description: Otters of the subfamily Lutrinae — semi-aquatic mustelids from rivers and coasts. Diversity, diet, social behaviour, and conservation context.

documents.name: Owl
documents.description: Owls (order Strigiformes): silent-flight nocturnal raptors. Diversity, habitats, hunting behaviour, hearing-based prey detection, and conservation context.

documents.name: Oxpecker
documents.description: Explore oxpeckers (genus Buphagus): African birds that ride on large mammals, feeding on ticks, insects, and blood — a relationship that is part cleaning service, part parasite.

documents.name: Oyster
documents.description: Learn about oysters, marine bivalve molluscs like the eastern and Pacific oyster, including their shells, filter feeding, reef-building role, and ecology.

documents.name: Paca
documents.description: Explore the paca (Cuniculus paca): a large, spotted, nocturnal Neotropical rodent with unique resonating cheekbones — a seed-disperser and one of the region's prized game animals.

documents.name: Paddlefish
documents.description: Explore paddlefish (family Polyodontidae): ancient river fish with a long sensory paddle snout that filter plankton from the water — using the American paddlefish. Conservation concern.

documents.name: Painted Frog
documents.description: Explore painted frogs (genus Discoglossus): mottled Mediterranean frogs of an ancient lineage, with a round tongue they can't flick out — using the Mediterranean painted frog.

documents.name: Painted Lady
documents.description: Meet the painted lady (Vanessa cardui), one of the world's most widespread butterflies and a remarkable long-distance migrant that visits flowers for nectar.

documents.name: Greater Painted-snipe
documents.description: Meet the greater painted-snipe (Rostratula benghalensis): a secretive wetland wader — not a true snipe — in which the brighter, larger female courts the males and leaves them to raise the brood.

documents.name: Giant Panda
documents.description: Ailuropoda melanoleuca: the giant panda. Bamboo-based diet, montane forest habitat in central China, solitary lifestyle, and decades of conservation work.

documents.name: Pangolin
documents.description: Explore pangolins (order Pholidota): the scale-covered, ant- and termite-eating mammals of Africa and Asia, and why they are a major focus of conservation against illegal trade.

documents.name: Parrot
documents.description: An overview of parrots (order Psittaciformes): diverse tropical birds, strong beaks and zygodactyl feet, vocal learning, and conservation and pet-ownership context.

documents.name: Parrotfish
documents.description: Explore parrotfish (family Scaridae): colourful reef fish with a beak-like mouth that scrape algae from coral and, in doing so, produce much of the white sand on tropical beaches.

documents.name: Peacock
documents.description: The peacock is the male peafowl, famous for its iridescent display train. An educational profile of the Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus): appearance, diet, and behaviour.

documents.name: Peccary
documents.description: Explore peccaries (family Tayassuidae): pig-like, herd-living mammals of the Americas — not true pigs — with a scent gland on the back and a taste for cactus and tough plants.

documents.name: Pelican
documents.description: Pelicans are large waterbirds with a huge throat pouch for catching fish. A group-level overview using the brown pelican as a reference: habitat, diet, and behaviour.

documents.name: Penguin
documents.description: Spheniscidae: flightless aquatic seabirds of the Southern Hemisphere. Wing-propelled swimming, diet, breeding colonies, and current conservation pressures.

documents.name: Pig
documents.description: Domestic pig (Sus domesticus): an educational overview of the intelligent, omnivorous farm pig — rooting behaviour, social life, breeds, and the wild boar ancestry.

documents.name: Pigeon
documents.description: The pigeon (rock dove, Columba livia): an educational profile of the familiar city bird and its domesticated forms — appearance, diet, behaviour, and human history.

documents.name: Pilot Whale
documents.description: Explore pilot whales (genus Globicephala): large, deep-diving members of the dolphin family with exceptionally strong social bonds and high intelligence.

documents.name: Pine Marten
documents.description: Explore the European pine marten (Martes martes): an agile, tree-climbing member of the weasel family with a cream throat patch, a woodland hunter and fruit-eater.

documents.name: Pink River Dolphin
documents.description: Learn about the pink river dolphin or boto (Inia geoffrensis), an endangered freshwater dolphin of the Amazon and Orinoco river systems in South America.

documents.name: Piranha
documents.description: Explore piranhas (e.g. the red-bellied piranha, Pygocentrus nattereri): sharp-toothed South American freshwater fish that are far less ferocious than their fearsome reputation.

documents.name: Pitta
documents.description: Explore pittas (family Pittidae): dazzlingly multicoloured, short-tailed ground birds of Old World forests — shy 'jewel-thrushes' that hop in the leaf litter hunting worms and insects.

documents.name: Plated Lizard
documents.description: Meet the plated lizard (Gerrhosaurus): an African lizard clad in regular rows of bony, rectangular scales, with a flexible skin fold along each flank that lets its armoured body expand.

documents.name: Platypus
documents.description: The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) is an egg-laying Australian mammal with a duck-like bill. An educational profile of its rivers, diet, behaviour, and unusual biology.

documents.name: Poison Dart Frog
documents.description: Explore poison dart frogs (family Dendrobatidae): tiny, brilliantly coloured rainforest frogs of Central and South America whose skin toxins come from their wild diet.

documents.name: Polar Bear
documents.description: Learn about the polar bear (Ursus maritimus), a white-furred Arctic bear that depends on sea ice to hunt seals, listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN.

documents.name: Pollen Wasp
documents.description: Pollen wasps (subfamily Masarinae) are unusual wasps that feed larvae on pollen and nectar like bees. Learn their biology, range, and careful pollinator role.

documents.name: Porcupine
documents.description: Porcupines are quill-covered rodents. A group-level overview using the North American porcupine as a reference — habitat, diet, behaviour, and how their quills work.

documents.name: Porpoise
documents.description: Porpoises (family Phocoenidae) are small toothed whales with blunt, beakless heads and triangular fins — habitat, diet, behaviour, and how they differ from dolphins.

documents.name: Potoo
documents.description: Explore potoos (family Nyctibiidae): nocturnal birds of the Americas that disguise themselves as broken tree stumps by day and catch insects on the wing by night — using the great potoo.

documents.name: Pratincole
documents.description: Meet the pratincole (Glareola): an unusual wader that hawks insects on the wing like a giant swallow, with long pointed wings and a forked tail — a close relative of the running coursers.

documents.name: Praying Mantis
documents.description: Praying mantises are predatory insects with grasping forelegs. A group-level overview of Mantodea using the European mantis as a reference: ambush hunting and camouflage.

documents.name: Proboscis Monkey
documents.description: Explore the proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus): a big-nosed, pot-bellied monkey of Borneo's riverside forests that is a strong swimmer and leaf specialist. Endangered.

documents.name: Pronghorn
documents.description: Explore the pronghorn (Antilocapra americana): North America's fastest land mammal, a unique species of open western grasslands with branched horns and long-distance migrations.

documents.name: Puff Adder
documents.description: The puff adder (Bitis arietans) is a thick-bodied venomous viper found across parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Learn its appearance, habitat, diet, and ecology.

documents.name: Puffbird
documents.description: Explore puffbirds (family Bucconidae): stocky, large-headed Neotropical birds that perch motionless for long spells, then sally out to grab insects and small prey with a stout, hooked bill.

documents.name: Pufferfish
documents.description: Pufferfish can inflate their bodies and many are highly toxic. A group-level overview of the family Tetraodontidae: habitat, diet, defences, and strong safety caution.

documents.name: Puffin
documents.description: Meet the three puffins (genus Fratercula) — northern seabirds of the auk family that fly in air and swim by flapping their wings underwater, and that shed their bright bill plates after each breeding season.

documents.name: Python
documents.description: Explore pythons (family Pythonidae): non-venomous constricting snakes of Africa, Asia, and Australia, including some of the longest snakes in the world, in an educational overview.

documents.name: Resplendent Quetzal
documents.description: Explore the resplendent quetzal (Pharomachrus mocinno): a dazzling green-and-red bird of Central American cloud forests, with long tail streamers and deep cultural significance.

documents.name: Quokka
documents.description: Explore the quokka (Setonix brachyurus): a small, round-faced wallaby of Western Australia famed for its 'smile' — a herbivore best known from Rottnest Island, and Vulnerable in the wild.

documents.name: Quoll
documents.description: Explore quolls (genus Dasyurus): spotted, cat-sized marsupial carnivores of Australia and New Guinea — using the spotted-tailed quoll. Several species are threatened.

documents.name: Rabbit
documents.description: Rabbits in the wild and as pets: Oryctolagus cuniculus and related Leporidae, habitat, herbivorous diet, social burrow life, and responsible-ownership context.

documents.name: Raccoon
documents.description: Procyon lotor: the common raccoon. Distribution, urban-adaptable omnivore, dexterous forepaws, and cautious notes on wildlife rather than pet status.

documents.name: Rain Frog
documents.description: Meet the rain frogs (Breviceps): plump, round-bodied African burrowing frogs that can't really swim or leap, squeak when alarmed, and hatch straight into froglets with no free-swimming tadpole stage.

documents.name: Rat
documents.description: Group-level profile of the rats of the genus Rattus: the brown rat Rattus norvegicus and black rat Rattus rattus, how a rat differs from a mouse by proportion, and why wild, commensal and domestic rats are not the same animal.

documents.name: Rattlesnake
documents.description: Explore rattlesnakes (genera Crotalus and Sistrurus): venomous New World pit vipers famous for the warning rattle on their tail, in a careful educational overview.

documents.name: Raven
documents.description: The common raven (Corvus corax): an educational profile of this large, intelligent corvid — appearance, wide range, omnivorous diet, and behaviour, with crow comparison.

documents.name: Ray
documents.description: Rays are flattened cartilaginous fish related to sharks. A group-level overview of the batoids: body plan, habitat, diet, behaviour, and cautious safety notes.

documents.name: Red-backed Salamander
documents.description: Explore the red-backed salamander (Plethodon cinereus): a tiny, abundant, lungless woodland salamander that breathes through its skin and lays eggs on land — no water stage needed.

documents.name: Red Deer
documents.description: The Red Deer (Cervus elaphus) is one of the largest deer species, known for the stags' branched antlers and autumn roaring. Habitat, diet and ecology.

documents.name: Red-eyed Tree Frog
documents.description: Meet the red-eyed tree frog (Agalychnis callidryas), an arboreal Central American amphibian with red eyes and blue flanks. A calm, factual guide.

documents.name: Red Panda
documents.description: The red panda (Ailurus fulgens): an educational profile of this small Himalayan mammal — its bamboo-rich diet, mountain forest habitat, behaviour, and conservation context.

documents.name: Redback Spider
documents.description: The redback spider (Latrodectus hasselti) is a widespread Australian widow relative; the female has a red stripe and often lives near human structures.

documents.name: Reed Frog
documents.description: Explore reed frogs (genus Hyperolius): small, vividly patterned African frogs of reeds and wetlands, famous for variable colours, loud night choruses, and disc-tipped climbing toes.

documents.name: Reef Manta Ray
documents.description: Learn about the reef manta ray (Mobula alfredi), a large filter-feeding ray of Indo-Pacific reefs, its plankton diet, biology and Vulnerable IUCN status.

documents.name: Remora
documents.description: Explore remoras (family Echeneidae): 'sharksucker' fish with a flat suction disc on the head that lets them hitch rides on sharks, rays, turtles, and whales — a free lift and a free meal.

documents.name: Reticulated Python
documents.description: Learn about the reticulated python (Malayopython reticulatus), a non-venomous constricting snake of South and Southeast Asia and the world's longest snake.

documents.name: Rhea
documents.description: Learn about the rhea, a large flightless ratite bird of South American grasslands: its appearance, habitat, diet, behavior, ecology and conservation.

documents.name: Rhinoceros
documents.description: Explore the world's rhinoceroses: the five living species across Africa and Asia, the white rhino (Ceratotherium simum), how rhinos live and feed, and why poaching makes conservation urgent.

documents.name: Ribbon Worm
documents.description: Explore ribbon worms (phylum Nemertea): soft, unsegmented marine worms that catch prey by everting a long sticky (sometimes venomous) proboscis — and include perhaps the longest animal on Earth.

documents.name: Risso's Dolphin
documents.description: Explore Risso's dolphin (Grampus griseus): a robust, heavily scarred grey dolphin that hunts squid in deep water — an intelligent, social member of the dolphin family.

documents.name: Roadrunner
documents.description: Explore the greater roadrunner (Geococcyx californianus): a fast-running, ground-dwelling cuckoo of North American deserts that sprints after lizards, snakes, and insects.

documents.name: Robin
documents.description: The robin: an educational profile using the European robin (Erithacus rubecula) as a reference, with a clear note that the American robin is an unrelated species.

documents.name: African Rock Python
documents.description: The African rock python (Python sebae) is a large non-venomous constrictor of sub-Saharan Africa. Learn about its biology, habitat, diet, and ecology.

documents.name: Roe Deer
documents.description: Learn about the roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), a small European deer of woodland edges and farmland, known for its delayed embryonic implantation.

documents.name: Roller
documents.description: Explore rollers (family Coraciidae): brilliantly coloured Old World birds named for the males' acrobatic, rolling courtship flights — bold perch-hunters of insects and small prey.

documents.name: Rook
documents.description: The rook (Corvus frugilegus) is a highly social Eurasian farmland corvid. How to separate an adult rook from a carrion crow, why juveniles are harder, and how rookeries work.

documents.name: Saiga
documents.description: Explore the saiga (Saiga tatarica): a migratory Central Asian steppe antelope with an extraordinary bulbous nose — an Ice Age survivor that crashed to near-extinction and is now recovering.

documents.name: Saki Monkey
documents.description: Explore saki monkeys (genus Pithecia): shaggy, long-tailed Amazonian monkeys famous for huge leaps — using the white-faced saki, where males and females look strikingly different.

documents.name: Salamander
documents.description: Salamanders are tailed amphibians with moist skin. A group-level overview using the fire salamander as a reference — habitat, diet, and why amphibians should not be handled.

documents.name: Salmon
documents.description: Salmon are migratory fish famous for returning to spawn. A group-level overview using sockeye salmon as a reference: life cycle, habitat, diet, and conservation caution.

documents.name: Salp
documents.description: Explore salps (class Thaliacea): transparent, barrel-shaped ocean drifters that jet through the water filtering plankton, form long glowing chains — and are surprising relatives of vertebrates.

documents.name: Saltwater Crocodile
documents.description: Learn about the saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), the largest living reptile, its Indo-Pacific range, ecology, and IUCN Least Concern status.

documents.name: Sand Cat
documents.description: Explore the sand cat (Felis margarita): a small desert cat with broad ears and fur-soled feet, superbly adapted to extreme deserts — and able to live with almost no drinking water.

documents.name: Sandfish
documents.description: Meet the sandfish (Scincus scincus): a desert skink — a lizard, not a fish — that dives beneath the sand and 'swims' through it with smooth scales, a wedge-shaped snout, and fringed toes.

documents.name: Sandgrouse
documents.description: Explore sandgrouse (family Pteroclidae): plump, camouflaged desert birds whose males soak up water in specially adapted belly feathers and fly it back to their thirsty chicks.

documents.name: Sandhill Crane
documents.description: Learn about the Sandhill Crane (Antigone canadensis), a tall grey crane known for its red forehead, bugling call, and large migratory gatherings.

documents.name: Sarus Crane
documents.description: Learn about the sarus crane (Antigone antigone), the tallest flying bird, a large grey wetland crane of South and Southeast Asia, and its Vulnerable status.

documents.name: Saw-scaled Viper
documents.description: Learn about the saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus), a small venomous viper of dry regions named for the rasping warning sound it makes with its scales.

documents.name: Scallop
documents.description: Learn about scallops (family Pectinidae), fan-shaped bivalve molluscs that can swim by clapping their shells and have rows of tiny eyes along the mantle.

documents.name: Scarlet Ibis
documents.description: The scarlet ibis is a vivid red wading bird of coastal wetlands in parts of northern South America, with a long down-curved bill and diet-derived colour.

documents.name: Scorpion
documents.description: Explore scorpions (order Scorpiones): ancient arachnids with pincers and a venomous tail sting, mostly harmless to people, that glow under ultraviolet light.

documents.name: Screamer
documents.description: Explore screamers (family Anhimidae): large South American wetland birds related to waterfowl, named for their loud calls, with wing spurs and air-filled bones under the skin.

documents.name: Sea Anemone
documents.description: Explore sea anemones (order Actiniaria): soft-bodied, skeleton-less relatives of corals whose stinging tentacles catch prey — and famously shelter clownfish.

documents.name: Sea Cucumber
documents.description: Explore sea cucumbers (class Holothuroidea): soft, sausage-shaped echinoderms that clean the seafloor, and defend themselves by expelling their own sticky — or even toxic — insides.

documents.name: Sea Fan
documents.description: Explore sea fans (gorgonians, e.g. Gorgonia ventalina): flexible, fan-shaped soft corals that stand across the current to filter-feed on plankton.

documents.name: Sea Lion
documents.description: Sea lions are eared seals in the family Otariidae — a group, not one species. How external ear flaps and forward-rotating hind flippers set them apart from true seals.

documents.name: Sea Slug
documents.description: Sea slug is a broad name for shell-less marine gastropods like the sea hare Aplysia. Learn about their appearance, habitat, diet, behavior, and ecology.

documents.name: Sea Snake
documents.description: Explore sea snakes (and sea kraits): venomous marine reptiles superbly adapted to ocean life, with paddle-shaped tails — using the banded sea krait. Educational, not first-aid advice.

documents.name: Sea Spider
documents.description: Explore sea spiders (class Pycnogonida): bizarre marine arthropods so thin-bodied they digest and breathe through their legs — not true spiders, but a strange, ancient lineage of their own.

documents.name: Sea Squirt
documents.description: Explore sea squirts (class Ascidiacea): sac-like marine filter feeders that, despite looking like sponges, are surprisingly close relatives of backboned animals — including us.

documents.name: Sea Turtle
documents.description: Sea turtles are ancient ocean reptiles. A group-level overview using the green sea turtle as a reference species: ocean habitat, diet, nesting, and conservation.

documents.name: Sea Urchin
documents.description: Explore sea urchins (class Echinoidea): spiny, globe-shaped echinoderms that graze the seabed with a five-toothed mouth and shape kelp forests and reefs.

documents.name: Leafy Seadragon
documents.description: Explore the leafy seadragon (Phycodurus eques): an ornate relative of the seahorse, found only in southern Australia, camouflaged as drifting seaweed with leaf-like body fronds.

documents.name: Seagull (Gull)
documents.description: Explore gulls (family Laridae): adaptable, intelligent coastal birds — popularly called seagulls — that thrive from shorelines to cities, using the herring gull as a reference.

documents.name: Seahorse
documents.description: Seahorses are unusual upright fish where males carry the young. A group-level overview of the genus Hippocampus: habitat, feeding, breeding, and conservation caution.

documents.name: Seal
documents.description: An overview of true seals (family Phocidae): harbor seal as a reference species, marine mammal biology, breeding haul-outs, diet, and conservation context.

documents.name: Secretarybird
documents.description: Explore the secretarybird (Sagittarius serpentarius): a tall, long-legged bird of prey that hunts on foot across African grasslands, stamping on snakes and other prey. Endangered.

documents.name: Seriema
documents.description: Explore seriemas (family Cariamidae): tall, long-legged South American grassland birds that hunt snakes and lizards on foot — the last living relatives of an extinct group of 'terror birds'.

documents.name: Serval
documents.description: Explore the serval (Leptailurus serval): a slender, long-legged African wild cat with huge ears, famous for using sound to locate prey and a spectacular high, arcing pounce.

documents.name: Shark
documents.description: An overview of sharks: cartilaginous fish, sensory biology, the diversity of species from reef sharks to whale sharks, and current conservation pressures.

documents.name: Sheep
documents.description: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries): an educational overview of the woolly grazing ruminant — flocking behaviour, grazing diet, breeds, and farm context.

documents.name: Shipworm
documents.description: Learn about the shipworm, a wood-boring bivalve mollusc of the family Teredinidae, including its anatomy, tunneling behavior, ecology, and history at sea.

documents.name: Shoebill
documents.description: Explore the shoebill (Balaeniceps rex): a tall, prehistoric-looking bird of African swamps with a massive shoe-shaped bill, famed for standing statue-still to ambush lungfish. Vulnerable.

documents.name: Shrew
documents.description: Explore shrews (family Soricidae): tiny, frantic-living insectivores with a non-stop metabolism — using the common shrew as a reference. Not rodents, despite the resemblance.

documents.name: Shrimp
documents.description: Explore shrimp: small, widespread decapod crustaceans of fresh and salt water, from reef cleaner shrimp to deep-sea species, with a key role in aquatic food webs.

documents.name: Sifaka
documents.description: Explore sifakas (genus Propithecus): large leaping lemurs of Madagascar that 'dance' sideways across open ground — using Verreaux's sifaka as a reference. Many are threatened.

documents.name: Silkworm
documents.description: Learn about the silkworm (Bombyx mori), the fully domesticated larva of the silk moth, its mulberry diet, cocoon-spinning, and the history of sericulture.

documents.name: Siren
documents.description: Explore sirens (family Sirenidae): eel-like aquatic salamanders that keep feathery gills for life and have only front legs — including the giant 'leopard eel' reticulated siren named in 2018.

documents.name: Skink
documents.description: Explore skinks (family Scincidae): one of the largest lizard families — smooth-scaled, often short-limbed lizards — using the blue-tongued skink as a colourful reference.

documents.name: Skunk
documents.description: Explore skunks (family Mephitidae): black-and-white mammals of the Americas best known for the powerful spray they use as a defense, and their adaptable, omnivorous lives.

documents.name: Sloth
documents.description: Sloths are slow-moving tree-dwelling mammals of the Americas. A group-level overview using the brown-throated three-toed sloth as a reference — habitat, diet, and behaviour.

documents.name: Slow Loris
documents.description: Explore slow lorises (genus Nycticebus): slow-moving, big-eyed nocturnal primates of Asia — and rare venomous mammals — gravely threatened by the illegal pet trade.

documents.name: Slug
documents.description: Explore slugs: shell-less gastropod molluscs closely related to snails that glide on a muscular foot, recycle decaying matter, and play a real role in soil ecosystems.

documents.name: Snail
documents.description: Explore snails: shelled gastropod molluscs of land, fresh water, and sea that glide on a muscular foot, rasp food with a toothed tongue, and retreat into a coiled shell.

documents.name: Snailfish
documents.description: Snailfish (family Liparidae) are soft, scaleless fish ranging from tide pools to the deepest ocean trenches, including some of the deepest fish ever recorded.

documents.name: Snake
documents.description: Snakes (suborder Serpentes): legless reptiles with diverse habitats and diets. Cautious overview, with snakebite safety guidance kept conservative and vet-aware.

documents.name: Snakehead
documents.description: Explore snakeheads (family Channidae): air-breathing freshwater predators that can survive out of water and even wriggle overland — prized food in Asia, but damaging invaders elsewhere.

documents.name: Snapping Turtle
documents.description: Learn about the snapping turtle (Chelydra serpentina), a large freshwater reptile of North America: its habitat, diet, behavior, ecology and conservation.

documents.name: Snow Leopard
documents.description: Learn about the snow leopard (Panthera uncia), a Vulnerable big cat of the high mountains of Central and South Asia, its adaptations, diet, and conservation.

documents.name: Snow Petrel
documents.description: The snow petrel is a small, pure-white seabird of the Southern Ocean, breeding on Antarctic and subantarctic rock and strongly tied to sea ice.

documents.name: Snowy Owl
documents.description: Learn about the snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus), a large white Arctic owl that breeds on tundra, hunts by day, and moves south in irregular winter irruptions.

documents.name: Spadefoot Toad
documents.description: Explore spadefoot toads (families Pelobatidae and Scaphiopodidae): burrowing toads that dig backwards with spade-like feet and wait out dry spells underground, breeding in fast bursts.

documents.name: Sparrow
documents.description: Sparrows are small seed-eating songbirds. A group-level overview using the house sparrow (Passer domesticus) as a reference: appearance, habitat, and behaviour.

documents.name: Spectacled Bear
documents.description: Learn about the spectacled bear, or Andean bear, the only bear native to South America. Covers its cloud-forest habitat, plant-heavy diet, and IUCN status.

documents.name: Spider
documents.description: Spiders are eight-legged arachnids (not insects) that produce silk. A group-level overview of the order Araneae: webs, hunting, venom, and ecological role.

documents.name: Spider Monkey
documents.description: Explore spider monkeys (genus Ateles): long-limbed New World monkeys with a gripping prehensile tail and hook-like hands, acrobatic fruit-eaters of the rainforest canopy. Many are threatened.

documents.name: Spinner Dolphin
documents.description: Explore the spinner dolphin (Stenella longirostris): a small, slender, highly social dolphin famous for leaping and spinning through the air, with complex day-night rhythms.

documents.name: Spring Peeper
documents.description: Explore the spring peeper (Pseudacris crucifer): a tiny North American tree frog marked with an X on its back, whose ringing 'peep' chorus is a famous herald of spring.

documents.name: Springhare
documents.description: Explore the springhare (Pedetes capensis): a nocturnal African rodent that hops on long hind legs like a tiny kangaroo, lives in burrows, and even glows under UV light.

documents.name: Squid
documents.description: Squid are fast-swimming cephalopod molluscs. A group-level overview using the Caribbean reef squid as a reference: tentacles, jet propulsion, and ocean habitats.

documents.name: Squirrel
documents.description: Explore squirrels (family Sciuridae): tree squirrels, ground squirrels, and flying squirrels, their worldwide range, seed-caching diet, and adaptable behaviour.

documents.name: Stag Beetle
documents.description: Learn about the stag beetle (Lucanus cervus), one of Europe's largest beetles, its deadwood-dependent larvae, behaviour, ecology and Near Threatened status.

documents.name: Staghorn Coral
documents.description: Explore staghorn coral (Acropora cervicornis): a fast-growing, branching reef coral that builds thickets of habitat — and a Caribbean species now critically endangered.

documents.name: Starfish
documents.description: Starfish (sea stars) are five-armed marine echinoderms. A group-level overview: tube feet, seabed habitats, feeding, and the ability to regenerate arms.

documents.name: Stick Insect
documents.description: Explore stick insects (order Phasmatodea): plant-eating insects that mimic twigs and leaves so perfectly they vanish in plain sight — including some of the longest insects on Earth.

documents.name: Stoat (Ermine)
documents.description: Explore the stoat (Mustela erminea): a small, bold mustelid that turns white in winter (ermine), hunts prey larger than itself, and ranges across northern continents.

documents.name: Stonefish
documents.description: Explore stonefish (genus Synanceia): masterfully camouflaged reef fish widely considered the most venomous fish on Earth. An educational profile, not first-aid or medical advice.

documents.name: Stork
documents.description: Storks are tall, long-legged wading birds. A group-level overview using the white stork as a reference: wetland and grassland habitat, diet, migration, and behaviour.

documents.name: Sturgeon
documents.description: Explore sturgeons (family Acipenseridae): ancient, armored, long-lived fish that have changed little since the age of dinosaurs — slow-growing bottom-feeders, and among the most threatened animals.

documents.name: Sugar Glider
documents.description: Explore the sugar glider (Petaurus breviceps): a small, nocturnal, gliding marsupial of Australia and New Guinea that soars between trees on a furry membrane and lives in social groups.

documents.name: Sun bear
documents.description: Explore the sun bear (Helarctos malayanus): the world's smallest bear, a tree-climbing forest specialist of Southeast Asia with a long tongue and a pale chest patch.

documents.name: Sunbird
documents.description: Explore sunbirds (family Nectariniidae): small, dazzlingly iridescent nectar-feeding birds of Africa, Asia, and Australasia — the Old World counterparts of hummingbirds.

documents.name: Sunbittern
documents.description: Explore the sunbittern (Eurypyga helias): a secretive Neotropical riverside bird that flashes startling eye-like 'sunburst' patterns on its wings when threatened.

documents.name: Sungrebe
documents.description: Explore the sungrebe (Heliornis fulica): a small, secretive American waterbird — a finfoot — extraordinary for the male's ability to carry tiny chicks in skin pouches under his wings.

documents.name: Surinam Toad
documents.description: Explore the Surinam toad (Pipa pipa): an extraordinarily flat, fully aquatic South American frog whose young develop in pockets on the mother's back and pop out as tiny froglets.

documents.name: Swan
documents.description: Swans are large, long-necked waterfowl. A group-level overview using the mute swan (Cygnus olor) as a reference: wetland habitat, diet, and protective behaviour.

documents.name: Swift
documents.description: Explore swifts (family Apodidae): supremely aerial birds that eat, sleep, and mate in flight — using the common swift, which can stay airborne for months without landing.

documents.name: Takahe
documents.description: The takahe is a large flightless rail endemic to New Zealand, once thought extinct and rediscovered in 1948. Learn about its biology and conservation.

documents.name: Takin
documents.description: Meet the takin (Budorcas taxicolor): a massive goat-antelope of the eastern Himalayas and China, with a moose-like nose and an oily coat — and Bhutan's national animal.

documents.name: Tamandua
documents.description: Explore tamanduas (genus Tamandua): medium-sized tree-climbing anteaters of the Americas with a prehensile tail and a long sticky tongue for raiding ant and termite nests.

documents.name: Tamarin
documents.description: Explore tamarins (family Callitrichidae): small, often flamboyant South American monkeys — using the golden lion tamarin, a conservation success story still classed as Endangered.

documents.name: Tapir
documents.description: Tapirs are large browsing mammals with a short prehensile snout. A group-level overview using the South American tapir as a reference — habitat, diet, and conservation.

documents.name: Tarantula
documents.description: Explore tarantulas (family Theraphosidae): large, hairy spiders that are mostly calm and only mildly venomous to people, with surprising defences like flicking irritating hairs.

documents.name: Tardigrade (Water Bear)
documents.description: Explore tardigrades (phylum Tardigrada): microscopic eight-legged 'water bears' that can survive boiling, freezing, drying out, radiation, and even the vacuum of space by entering a dormant state.

documents.name: Tarsier
documents.description: Explore tarsiers (family Tarsiidae): tiny, huge-eyed nocturnal primates of Southeast Asia that are pure carnivores — using the Philippine tarsier as a reference.

documents.name: Tasmanian Devil
documents.description: Explore the Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii): the world's largest carnivorous marsupial — a powerful scavenger of Tasmania threatened by a contagious facial cancer.

documents.name: Tegu
documents.description: Explore tegus (genera Salvator, Tupinambis): large, intelligent South American lizards — using the Argentine black-and-white tegu, which is unusual for being partly warm-bodied.

documents.name: Tenrec
documents.description: Explore tenrecs (family Tenrecidae): a diverse group of small Madagascan mammals that mimic hedgehogs, shrews, and otters — using the spiny lowland streaked tenrec as a reference.

documents.name: Termite
documents.description: Explore termites (order Isoptera): social insects that recycle dead wood and build towering mounds — sometimes pests, but vital ecosystem engineers, and actually a kind of cockroach.

documents.name: Tetra
documents.description: Tetras are small schooling fish popular in aquariums. A group-level overview using the neon tetra as a reference species: appearance, habitat, and shoaling behaviour.

documents.name: Thick-knee (Stone-curlew)
documents.description: Explore thick-knees or stone-curlews (family Burhinidae): cryptic, large-eyed, mostly nocturnal ground birds named for their knobbly leg joints — masters of camouflage and eerie night calls.

documents.name: Thorny Devil
documents.description: Explore the thorny devil (Moloch horridus): a spiky Australian desert lizard that eats only ants, channels dew to its mouth through its skin, and is completely harmless despite its look.

documents.name: Thrips
documents.description: Explore thrips (order Thysanoptera): tiny slender insects with unique fringed wings that feed by rasping plant cells — important pollinators and pests, where one bug is also a 'thrips'.

documents.name: Tick
documents.description: Ticks are eight-legged arachnids in the order Ixodida that feed on blood. Learn about their biology, life cycle, questing behaviour, and habitats here.

documents.name: Tiger
documents.description: Panthera tigris: the largest living cat. Where tigers live, what they hunt, why they are solitary, and the conservation pressures they face across Asia.

documents.name: Tiger Salamander
documents.description: Explore the tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum): one of the largest land salamanders in North America — a burrowing, blotched amphibian and close relative of the axolotl.

documents.name: Tilapia
documents.description: Learn about tilapia, the freshwater cichlid fishes including the Nile tilapia, their native African waters, algae-rich diet, and mouthbrooding behaviour.

documents.name: Tinamou
documents.description: Explore tinamous (family Tinamidae): plump, ground-dwelling South American birds related to the flightless ratites, known for glossy enamel-like eggs and role-reversed parenting.

documents.name: Titi Monkey
documents.description: Explore titi monkeys (genera Plecturocebus, Callicebus, Cheracebus): small South American monkeys famous for devoted lifelong pairs that twine their tails together.

documents.name: Toad
documents.description: Toads are warty-skinned amphibians, a kind of frog. A group-level overview using the common toad as a reference — habitat, diet, and why amphibians should not be handled.

documents.name: Tody
documents.description: Explore todies (family Todidae): minuscule, big-headed, emerald-green Caribbean birds with red throats that dart out to snatch insects — among the smallest birds of the West Indies.

documents.name: Tokay Gecko
documents.description: Explore the tokay gecko (Gekko gecko): a large, boldly spotted Asian gecko famous for its loud 'to-kay' call, powerful bite, and amazing toe pads that let it cling to almost anything.

documents.name: Tomato Frog
documents.description: Explore the tomato frog (Dyscophus antongilii): a plump, tomato-red frog found only in Madagascar that puffs up and oozes a sticky, irritating glue when threatened.

documents.name: Tortoise
documents.description: Explore tortoises (family Testudinidae): land-dwelling, shelled reptiles known for long lifespans and herbivorous diets, from giant island tortoises to small desert species.

documents.name: Toucan
documents.description: Toucans are tropical birds with huge, colourful bills. A group-level overview using the toco toucan as a reference: rainforest habitat, fruit diet, and behaviour.

documents.name: Tree Frog
documents.description: Explore tree frogs: climbing frogs with sticky toe pads found across several families, from the vivid red-eyed tree frog to small grey species, in an educational overview.

documents.name: Tree Kangaroo
documents.description: Learn about tree kangaroos (genus Dendrolagus), arboreal macropods of New Guinea and northeastern Australia, their habitat, diet, and conservation.

documents.name: Triggerfish
documents.description: Explore triggerfish (family Balistidae): boldly patterned reef fish with a locking dorsal spine and powerful teeth — clever foragers, and famously fierce nest-guarders.

documents.name: Trogon
documents.description: Explore trogons (family Trogonidae): brilliantly coloured tropical forest birds — including the famous quetzals — that sit motionless, swivel their toes oddly, and nest in tree holes.

documents.name: Tropicbird
documents.description: Explore tropicbirds (family Phaethontidae): elegant white seabirds of tropical oceans with long tail streamers that plunge-dive for fish and nest on remote islands.

documents.name: Trumpeter
documents.description: Explore trumpeters (genus Psophia): rounded, social ground birds of Amazonian forests named for their deep trumpeting calls, with unusually cooperative group lives.

documents.name: Tsetse Fly
documents.description: Learn about the tsetse fly (genus Glossina), a blood-feeding African insect, its biology, unusual reproduction, ecology, and public-health context.

documents.name: Tuatara
documents.description: Explore the tuatara (Sphenodon punctatus): a reptile from New Zealand that is the sole survivor of an ancient order, often called a living fossil, with a famously slow pace of life.

documents.name: Tuna
documents.description: Tuna are fast, powerful open-ocean fish. A group-level overview using bluefin and yellowfin as references: speed, warm-bodied biology, range, and conservation caution.

documents.name: Turaco
documents.description: Explore turacos (family Musophagidae): colourful African fruit-eating birds with truly green and red feather pigments found in almost no other birds — using the great blue turaco.

documents.name: Turtle
documents.description: Turtles, tortoises, and terrapins (order Testudines): shelled reptiles across freshwater, marine, and terrestrial habitats, with cautious conservation context.

documents.name: Uakari
documents.description: Explore uakaris (genus Cacajao): short-tailed Amazonian monkeys, the bald uakari famous for a bright crimson face that signals health — a flooded-forest seed specialist. Vulnerable.

documents.name: Umbrellabird
documents.description: Explore umbrellabirds (genus Cephalopterus): large black Neotropical cotingas with an umbrella-like crest and a long throat wattle, whose males boom to attract mates.

documents.name: Vampire Squid
documents.description: Meet the vampire squid (Vampyroteuthis infernalis), a small, gentle deep-sea cephalopod that drifts in the oxygen-minimum zone and feeds on sinking marine snow.

documents.name: Velvet Worm
documents.description: Explore velvet worms (phylum Onychophora): ancient, soft-bodied land animals with stubby legs that hunt by firing jets of sticky slime to ensnare prey — a lineage half a billion years old.

documents.name: Vicuna
documents.description: The vicuna is a wild camelid of the high Andes, famous for its fine wool and conservation recovery. Learn about its habitat, behavior, and ecology.

documents.name: Viper
documents.description: Explore vipers (family Viperidae): heavy-bodied venomous snakes with long hinged fangs and superb camouflage — using the Gaboon viper. An educational profile, not first-aid advice.

documents.name: Vulture
documents.description: Vultures are scavenging birds vital to ecosystems. A group-level overview using the turkey vulture as a reference, distinguishing New World and Old World vultures.

documents.name: Wall Lizard
documents.description: Explore wall lizards (genus Podarcis): small, quick, sun-loving European lizards that scamper over walls, rocks, and ruins — adaptable enough to thrive right alongside people.

documents.name: Wallaby
documents.description: Learn about wallabies, small-to-medium hopping marsupials of the family Macropodidae found in parts of Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands.

documents.name: Walrus
documents.description: Explore the walrus (Odobenus rosmarus): a huge, tusked Arctic marine mammal that hauls out in great herds, dives for clams, and depends on sea ice and shallow seas.

documents.name: Wandering Albatross
documents.description: Learn about the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), a vast Southern Ocean seabird with an enormous wingspan that breeds on subantarctic islands.

documents.name: Warthog
documents.description: Explore the common warthog (Phacochoerus africanus): a wild pig of African savannas, its burrowing habits, grazing diet, tusks, and how it lives alongside larger wildlife.

documents.name: Wasp
documents.description: Explore wasps (order Hymenoptera): diverse insects from social yellowjackets to solitary species — feared for their sting, but vital predators of pests and useful pollinators.

documents.name: Weasel
documents.description: Explore weasels (genus Mustela): small, slender, fast-moving carnivores of the weasel family, including the least weasel — the smallest carnivoran in the world.

documents.name: Weaver
documents.description: Explore weavers (family Ploceidae): small, often bright-yellow Old World birds famous for elaborately woven, knotted nests — using the southern masked weaver as a reference.

documents.name: Weddell Seal
documents.description: The Weddell Seal lives on Antarctic fast ice, diving deep under the ice to hunt fish and squid. Learn about its biology, habitat, and conservation.

documents.name: Wedge-tailed Eagle
documents.description: Learn about the wedge-tailed eagle, Australia's largest bird of prey: its appearance, habitat across mainland Australia and Tasmania, diet and ecology.

documents.name: Weeverfish
documents.description: Meet the weeverfish (Trachinidae): a small, sand-burying coastal fish with venomous spines that is among the most venomous fish in temperate European waters — and a hazard to barefoot beachgoers.

documents.name: Weevil
documents.description: Explore weevils (family Curculionidae): snout-faced beetles that make up one of the largest animal families on Earth — mostly plant-eaters, including some notorious crop pests.

documents.name: Whale
documents.description: Whales as marine mammals (infraorder Cetacea). Baleen and toothed whale split, humpback whale as a reference, vocalisation, migration, and conservation context.

documents.name: Whelk
documents.description: Learn about whelks, marine gastropod sea snails like the common whelk (Buccinum undatum): their spiral shells, predatory feeding, habitat, and ecology.

documents.name: Whiptail Lizard
documents.description: Explore whiptail lizards (genus Aspidoscelis): slender, striped, long-tailed New World racers — famous because several species are all-female and reproduce by cloning (parthenogenesis).

documents.name: White Stork
documents.description: Learn about the White Stork (Ciconia ciconia), a large white-and-black wading bird that nests in parts of Europe and migrates to sub-Saharan Africa.

documents.name: Whooping Crane
documents.description: The whooping crane is North America's tallest bird, an endangered wetland species and one of the world's most intensively managed conservation recoveries.

documents.name: Wild boar
documents.description: Explore the wild boar (Sus scrofa): the wild ancestor of domestic pigs, a highly adaptable omnivore of Eurasian forests now found across much of the world.

documents.name: Wild Turkey
documents.description: Learn about the Wild Turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), a large ground-dwelling bird of North American woodlands, its biology, ecology, and conservation status.

documents.name: Wildebeest
documents.description: Explore the wildebeest (genus Connochaetes): large African antelopes known for vast migrating herds, grassland grazing, and their central role in savanna ecosystems.

documents.name: Wolf
documents.description: Canis lupus: wolf habitat and range, pack social structure, hunting behaviour, the relationship with domestic dogs, and conservation context.

documents.name: Wolffish
documents.description: Explore wolffish (genus Anarhichas): big, blunt-faced cold-water fish with fearsome fangs and crushing teeth for eating shellfish — and natural antifreeze proteins that keep their blood flowing.

documents.name: Wolverine
documents.description: Explore the wolverine (Gulo gulo): the largest land member of the weasel family, a powerful, far-ranging carnivore of northern forests and tundra.

documents.name: Wombat
documents.description: Wombats are stocky burrowing marsupials of Australia. A group-level overview using the common wombat as a reference — habitat, grazing diet, burrows, and behaviour.

documents.name: Wood Frog
documents.description: Explore the wood frog (Lithobates sylvaticus): a masked North American frog that can freeze nearly solid each winter — heart stopped — and thaw back to life in spring, ranging into the Arctic.

documents.name: Woodlouse
documents.description: Explore woodlice (suborder Oniscidea): the only crustaceans fully adapted to life on land — armoured, harmless decomposers (pill bugs and sow bugs) that recycle dead plant matter.

documents.name: Woodpecker
documents.description: Woodpeckers are tree-climbing birds that drum and chisel into wood. A group-level overview using the great spotted woodpecker as a reference: habitat, diet, and behaviour.

documents.name: Woolly Monkey
documents.description: Explore woolly monkeys (genus Lagothrix): thickset, woolly-furred Amazon monkeys with a strong prehensile tail — important fruit-eating seed dispersers, and threatened by hunting.

documents.name: Worm Lizard
documents.description: Explore worm lizards (Amphisbaenia): ringed, mostly legless burrowing reptiles that look like big earthworms — neither worms nor true snakes, but a distinct group of squamates.

documents.name: Wrasse
documents.description: Explore wrasses (family Labridae): a huge family of colourful reef fish — from tiny cleaner wrasses to the giant humphead wrasse — many of which can change sex during their lives.

documents.name: Yeti Crab
documents.description: Yeti crabs (genus Kiwa) are pale, hairy deep-sea squat lobsters that live near hydrothermal vents and seeps and appear to farm chemosynthetic bacteria.

documents.name: Zebra
documents.description: Equus: three species of African equids. Stripes, habitats from plains to mountain to arid, herd behaviour, grazing ecology, and conservation context.

documents.name: Zorilla
documents.description: Meet the zorilla or striped polecat (Ictonyx striatus): an African mustelid that looks and smells like a skunk through convergent evolution, but is not a skunk at all.

facets.label: Animal group
facets.description: The section of the encyclopedia an animal is filed under. These are FaunaHub's shelves, not strict taxonomy — whales and seals sit under Marine Animals, sharks under Fish.

facets.label: Taxonomic group
facets.description: Class- and phylum-level groups from FaunaHub's taxonomy registry. Finer than the encyclopedia shelves — amphibians separate from reptiles, molluscs from insects.

facets.label: What FaunaHub has
facets.description: Refine by what this site publishes for an animal. These are facts about FaunaHub's own coverage, checked for every profile.

excludedFacets.label: Continent
excludedFacets.reason: The fauna geography registry covers land, freshwater and coastal species by design and excludes purely marine ones, so a continent filter would silently omit a large part of the collection rather than report it as unknown.

excludedFacets.label: Habitat
excludedFacets.reason: Habitat tags exist only on the profiles the fauna geography registry covers. Filtering on them would present a partial editorial pass as a property of the animal.

excludedFacets.label: Ocean depth zone
excludedFacets.reason: Recorded only for the marine species on the ocean depth pages.

excludedFacets.label: Diet
excludedFacets.reason: Present on most profiles, but as a written sentence rather than a category. Sorting those sentences into carnivore, herbivore and omnivore would be assigning a classification the editors never made.

excludedFacets.label: Class (taxon)
excludedFacets.reason: Written freely, often with a parenthetical gloss, so the same class appears under several spellings. The taxonomy registry carries the same information already normalised.

excludedFacets.label: Habitat (written)
excludedFacets.reason: A description of where the animal lives, not a category it belongs to.

excludedFacets.label: Activity pattern
excludedFacets.reason: Recorded on too few profiles, and as prose rather than a category.

excludedFacets.label: Conservation status
excludedFacets.reason: FaunaHub's Red List records are a genuine IUCN enum, but only a handful are joined to an encyclopedia profile. The conservation category pages under /endangered-animals are where that data is complete.

excludedFacets.label: Domestic or wild
excludedFacets.reason: The domestication registry is a reviewed list of domesticated animals. Everything absent from it defaults to wild WITHOUT having been individually checked, so offering a wild/domestic toggle would imply an audit that has not happened. The documented half is offered as a coverage refinement instead.
